The name MLMVPN is derived from its advanced core architecture: the Multi-Layer Multiplexer. We have pushed the boundaries of traditional networking by designing an ultra-intelligent, multi-layered platform instead of relying on a single connection. By simultaneously orchestrating several powerful anti-censorship engines, this application dynamically routes your traffic through the fastest and most secure paths available. Our mission is to provide a highly stable and ultra-fast network that shatters internet restrictions across multiple layers, delivering an unparalleled and truly free web experience.

After connecting, why does it say “route verified (WARP)” and not show a country?

Because it is not accurate. We tested it on a list of 2,827 servers: the IP database agreed with the country the server itself declared only 34% of the time. Cloudflare addresses are registered in the United States but answer from Frankfurt, and OVH and Oracle ranges are registered in one country and served from another — a database tells you where a range is registered, not where it answers from. Instead we read the country from the server\'s own name (instantly, with no internet) and correct it with a real measurement after connecting.

Because the app used to send QUIC traffic (the newer protocol YouTube and Instagram try first) into the tunnel, and Cloudflare workers do not carry that kind of traffic at all. So every video stalled for a few hundred milliseconds, failed, and then retried the ordinary way. In the new version that traffic is rejected immediately so it goes straight down the right path. Game and voice-call traffic is left untouched.

Because when the route goes through Cloudflare WARP, Cloudflare deliberately reports your own country rather than the server\'s — so a connection from Tehran that really exits in Frankfurt is reported as “Iran”. That is why no country is recorded in this case; otherwise every server would be wrongly filed under the Iranian flag. Your connection is perfectly fine, the exit country simply cannot be proven this way.

What it changes: your ISP's resolver can see every name you look up, and on many networks it also answers with the wrong address on purpose — the block you are trying to get past often starts here rather than at the connection itself. Setting a resolver of your own takes that tool away from them.

You can enter more than one, separated by commas — the first goes on the tunnel interface, and the whole list is handed to the transports as the resolvers to use inside the tunnel. There the resolver decides more than privacy: a CDN answers with a server near whoever asked, so a resolver in the country you exit through is what gets you a nearby node instead of one back at the gateway.

If pages stop loading after you change this, the resolver you typed is not reachable — put it back to 1.1.1.1.

With the current value of %1$d:

When you need it: to send one program through the tunnel instead of the whole phone (turn on Proxy mode), or to let a PC on the same Wi-Fi use this phone's tunnel (turn on LAN access). In both cases you enter this phone's address and this port on the other side.

Every engine uses the same port, so a proxy you configure once keeps working whichever tunnel you switch to.

Change it only if something else on the phone already holds this port. If a value is refused, the message says why.

Off (the default): the whole phone goes through the tunnel and the engine takes the network interface directly. Every app is covered without doing anything, which is what almost everyone wants.
On: the engine publishes a local proxy on the port above. What that means for the rest of the phone depends on which engine is running, and the difference is worth knowing.
With the Xray family (VLESS, VMess, Trojan, Shadowsocks, Reality) there is no device-wide tunnel at all: traffic goes through the proxy ONLY from programs you have pointed at that port by hand, and everything else keeps using your normal connection, uncovered.
With MASQUE, WireGuard and WARP-on-WARP the whole phone stays tunnelled — the traffic simply reaches the engine through that local proxy instead of through the interface. Nothing is left uncovered.
The reason to turn it on: a local proxy is the only thing another device can connect to, so this is what makes Local Network sharing possible for MASQUE, WireGuard and WARP-on-WARP.
The trap, and it only applies to the Xray family: with this on, the app can look connected while your browser is not going through it at all. If you turn it on and things stop being unblocked, that is why — the proxy is running and nothing is pointed at it.
The per-app list in Advanced VPN is the other way round and is often the better tool: it keeps the device-wide tunnel and simply leaves the apps you choose outside it.

On (the default): the proxy listens on every network interface, so another device on the same Wi-Fi or hotspot can use this phone's tunnel. Point it at this phone's local address on port %1$d.

What it is good for: a laptop or a TV with no VPN of its own, or a PC you would rather not install anything on. Tether the phone or put both on the same Wi-Fi, set the proxy on the other device, and it is covered.

What it costs, stated plainly: the proxy has no password. Anyone who can reach this phone on the network can use it — and their traffic then leaves through your tunnel and counts as yours. On your own hotspot that is only the devices you tethered. On a café, hotel, airport or office Wi-Fi it is everyone on that network.

Turn it off when you are on a network you do not control and are not deliberately sharing. With it off the proxy is reachable only from this phone.
